planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Rebecca's Gold predates the modern Peterson Pawpaw releases and sets its best crops when planted with a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Rebecca's Gold is one of the older named pawpaw selections, predating the modern Peterson Pawpaw cultivars and long maintained in pawpaw germplasm collections for its rich, deep-golden flesh and excellent sweet flavor. It is a productive, reliable tree that has stood the test of decades of cultivation among pawpaw enthusiasts and collectors, valued alongside historic selections like Overleese and Sunflower as part of the foundation on which today's larger-fruited cultivars were bred. As with all pawpaws, Rebecca's Gold is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set; hand-pollinating between two open flowers of different cultivars with a small brush can improve yield where natural fly and beetle pollinators are scarce. Provide consistent moisture through the first two seasons while the shallow root system establishes, and expect the tree to fruit within four to eight years from a grafted start.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Sevillano benefits from a second olive cultivar such as Manzanillo or Mission nearby for improved fruit set, and needs a large mature footprint compared with compact cultivars like Arbequina.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Sevillano is a Spanish-origin olive cultivar known in California and other American growing regions as the classic large-fruited table olive, producing some of the biggest olives of any commonly grown cultivar — prized for canning and curing as whole table olives rather than for oil, where its low oil content is a disadvantage. Trees are vigorous and grow considerably larger than compact modern cultivars like Arbequina, so give Sevillano plenty of room to reach its full spreading form. Harvest green for classic Spanish-style brine-cured green olives, or allow fruit to ripen to black for a milder cured product; either way, fresh-picked olives are intensely bitter and must be cured in lye or long brine soaks before they are palatable. Sevillano is only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second olive cultivar nearby improves both fruit set and yield. Established trees are drought-tolerant and long-lived, tolerating the alkaline, low-fertility soils typical of much of the Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Leccino is partially self-fruitful but bears more heavily with a second cultivar such as Frantoio or Pendolino nearby, and is among the more cold-tolerant Italian olive cultivars available.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Leccino is one of Italy's most widely planted olive cultivars, valued for producing smooth, mild, buttery oil with low bitterness and pungency compared to more robust Tuscan cultivars like Frantoio, and for its comparatively good tolerance of cold winters and root rot among Italian olive selections, which has made it a popular choice in warm-temperate American olive trials including in the Southeast. Trees are vigorous, spreading, and heavy-bearing, typically beginning meaningful production within four to six years of planting. Harvest olives from green through purple-black depending on the oil style desired — earlier harvest yields a greener, more peppery oil, while later harvest gives a milder, more buttery result. Leccino is only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and yield. Established trees tolerate drought and poor, alkaline soil well, needing supplemental water mainly during the first two years and during fruit development in dry summers.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas

common_name: Ascolano Olive (Large Mild Table and Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Ascolano bears more reliably with a second olive cultivar such as Manzanillo or Mission nearby for cross-pollination, and has thinner skin than most table olives, so handle fruit gently at harvest.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Ascolano is an Italian-origin olive cultivar long grown in California for its large, thin-skinned, mild-flavored fruit — one of the highest-quality table olives available, with less bitterness before curing than most cultivars and flesh that separates easily from the pit. Its thin skin bruises more readily than firmer-skinned table olives such as Manzanillo or Sevillano, so fruit is best hand-harvested carefully rather than shaken or mechanically picked. Ascolano can be cured green or ripe black and also produces good-quality oil, though its lower oil content and thinner skin make it less common in commercial oil orchards. Trees are moderately vigorous and only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and overall yield. As with other olives, established Ascolano trees are notably drought-tolerant and adapt well to the alkaline, low-fertility soils common across much of the Gulf Coast and Texas.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas

common_name: Coratina Olive (High-Polyphenol Southern Italian Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Coratina is largely self-fruitful but produces a heavier crop with a second cultivar such as Frantoio or Leccino nearby, and is a vigorous grower that tolerates heat well.

directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Coratina is a Southern Italian olive cultivar from Puglia prized for producing intensely robust, bitter, peppery oil with exceptionally high polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown olive cultivar — making it a favorite for growers and consumers seeking a bold, health-forward oil rather than a mild table experience. The tree is vigorous, heat-tolerant, and productive, and has performed well in warm-climate US oil-olive trials outside its native Mediterranean range, including in parts of the Southeast. Harvest early, while fruit is still green to just turning color, for the most intensely peppery, high-polyphenol oil; later harvest mellows the flavor but reduces polyphenol content. Coratina is largely self-fruitful, though yields improve with a second compatible cultivar nearby. Established trees are drought-tolerant and, like most olives, thrive on benign neglect once past the first two establishment years, needing supplemental water mainly during prolonged dry spells at fruit set.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Olive Production in Texas
